text:
Book 2

The Assembly of Ithaca's People — Speeches by Telemachus and the Suitors — Telemachus Prepares to Sail to Pylos with Athena, Disguised as Mentor

As rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Telemachus woke up and got dressed. He tied sandals onto his feet and fastened his sword to his shoulder. He left his room, looking as majestic as an immortal god. He immediately sent heralds to call the people to an assembly. The heralds called, and everyone gathered. Once everyone was there, Telemachus headed to the assembly, spear in hand. He wasn't alone; his two hunting dogs walked beside him. Athena gave him such a divine grace that everyone who saw him was amazed. When he took his father's seat, even the oldest council members made way for him.

Aegyptius, a man bent with age but full of wisdom, was the first to speak. His son, Antiphus, had gone with Odysseus to Troy, the land of fine horses. But when they were trapped in the Cyclops' cave, the cruel monster killed Antiphus and made him his last meal. Aegyptius still had three sons. Two of them worked on their father's land, and the third, Eurynomus, was one of the suitors. Despite this, Aegyptius couldn't get over the loss of Antiphus. He was still weeping for him as he began his speech.

He began,

"People of Ithaca, listen to my words! Since Odysseus left us, our council hasn't met once. Who, young or old, felt it so important to call us together now? Has someone heard news of an enemy army approaching and wants to warn us? Or is there some other important public matter to discuss? I'm sure it's a good person, and I pray Zeus grants them their heart's desire."

Telemachus took this speech as a good sign. He had so much to say that he felt like he would burst, so he stood up at once. He stood in the middle of the assembly, and the good herald Pisenor handed him his staff. Then, he turned to Aegyptius and spoke.

"Sir, you'll soon learn that I'm the one who called this meeting, because I am suffering the most. I haven't heard news of an enemy army, and I'm not here to warn you about public matters. My pain is purely personal, caused by two great misfortunes that have struck my house. First, there's the loss of my excellent father. He was the best among all of you here, like a father to each one of you. Second, and far more serious, is something that will soon completely ruin my estate. The sons of all your leading men are constantly pestering my mother to marry them, even though she doesn't want to. They're afraid to go to her father, Icarius, and ask him to choose a son-in-law and provide wedding gifts for his daughter. Instead, they hang around my father's house every day. They slaughter our oxen, sheep, and fat goats for their feasts, and they don't even think about how much wine they drink. No estate can withstand such recklessness! Now, there's no Odysseus to protect our home from harm. I don't have the power to stop them. I'll never be as great a man as my father was. But if I had the strength, I would defend myself! I can't stand this treatment any longer. My house is being disgraced and ruined. So, respect your own consciences and public opinion. Also, fear the wrath of the gods! They might be displeased and turn against you. I beg you, in the name of Zeus and Themis, who guide all councils, my friends, don't leave me to face this alone! Unless, of course, my brave father Odysseus did some wrong to the Achaeans, and you're now helping these suitors to get revenge on me. What's more, if my house is to be completely devoured, I'd rather you did the eating yourselves. Then I could take action against you, sending notices to each of your homes until I got everything back. But now, I have no way to get justice."

After saying this, Telemachus threw his staff to the ground and burst into tears. Everyone felt deeply sorry for him, but they all remained seated and silent. Only Antinous dared to answer, his voice full of anger.

"Telemachus, you arrogant braggart! How dare you try to blame us suitors? This isn't our fault; it's your mother's. She's a very cunning woman. For three years, almost four, she's been driving us crazy! She encourages each of us, sends messages, but never means a single word. Then there was another trick she played on us. She set up a huge weaving loom in her room and started working on an enormous, intricate piece of embroidery. She told us, 'My dear suitors, Odysseus is truly dead. But don't pressure me to remarry right away. Please wait until I finish weaving a burial shroud for the noble Laertes, for when death finally takes him. He's a very wealthy man, and the women of the town will gossip if he's buried without a shroud.'

"We agreed to her request. We watched her work on her great fabric all day long, but at night, by torchlight, she would unpick the stitches again. She fooled us like this for three years, and we never found out! But as time passed, and she was in her fourth year, one of her maids, who knew what she was doing, told us the truth. We caught her in the act of undoing her work, so she had to finish it, whether she wanted to or not. So, the suitors give you this answer, so both you and the Achaeans can understand: 'Send your mother away, and tell her to marry the man she and her father choose.' I don't know what will happen if she keeps tormenting us much longer with the airs she puts on, thanks to the skills Athena taught her and her own cleverness. We've never heard of such a woman! We know all about Tyro, Alcmena, Mycene, and the famous women of old, but none of them compare to your mother. It wasn't fair of her to treat us that way. As long as she keeps the stubborn mind the gods have given her, we will continue to devour your estate. I don't see why she should change, since she gets all the honor and glory, and you're the one paying for it, not her! So understand this: we won't return to our own lands, here or anywhere else, until she makes her choice and marries one of us."
Telemachus replied,

"Antinous, and all you other suitors, how can I possibly drive my own mother, who gave birth to me, out of my father's house? My father is far away, and we don't know if he's alive or dead. If I insist on sending my mother back to her father, Icarius, I'd have to pay him a huge sum of money, and that would be incredibly difficult for me. Not only would he treat me harshly, but the heavens would punish me too! My mother, if she left this house, would call upon the Furies to avenge her. Besides, it wouldn't be an honorable thing to do, and I want nothing to do with it. If you're offended by what I'm saying, then leave this house! Go feast at each other's homes, taking turns, and pay for it yourselves. But if you choose to keep freeloading off one man, then may the heavens help me, but Zeus will make you pay in full! And when you fall in my father's house, there will be no one to avenge you!"

As he spoke, Zeus sent two eagles from the mountaintop. The eagles soared on the wind, flying side by side in a majestic flight. When they reached the center of the assembly, they circled and wheeled. Their wings beat the air, and they glared down at the people below as if ready to kill. Then, fighting fiercely and tearing at each other, they flew off to the right, over the city. The people watched in amazement, asking each other what this could mean. Then Halitherses, the best prophet and interpreter of omens among them, spoke to them plainly and honestly.

"People of Ithaca, listen to me! I speak especially to the suitors, for I see trouble brewing for them. Odysseus won't be away much longer. In fact, he's close by, ready to bring death and destruction. This won't just be for the suitors, but for many of us who live in Ithaca. So, let's be wise before it's too late. Let's stop this wickedness before he arrives. It would be better for the suitors to do this on their own. I'm not prophesying without knowing what I'm talking about. Everything I foretold for Odysseus when the Argives set out for Troy, and he with them, has come true. I said that after suffering great hardship and losing all his men, he would return home in his twentieth year, and no one would recognize him. Now, all of this is becoming reality!"
Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke up.

"Go home, old man! Prophesy to your own children, or something worse might happen to them! I can interpret these omens much better than you can. Birds are always flying around in the sunshine, but they rarely mean anything important. Odysseus died in a faraway land. It's a shame you're not dead with him, instead of babbling about omens here and fueling Telemachus's anger, which is already fierce enough! I suppose you think Telemachus will give your family something. But I'm telling you, and it will surely happen: when an old man like you, who should know better, stirs up a young man until he becomes troublesome, first, that young friend will only suffer more. He'll gain nothing, because the suitors will stop him. And second, we'll impose a heavier fine on you, sir, than you'll ever want to pay, because it will be a great burden on you. As for Telemachus, I warn him in front of all of you: send his mother back to her father! Her father will find her a husband and provide her with all the wedding gifts a beloved daughter can expect. Until then, we will continue to harass him with our suit. We fear no man, and we don't care about his fancy speeches or any of your fortune-telling! You can preach all you want, but we'll only hate you more! We'll go back and keep eating up Telemachus's estate without paying him, until his mother stops tormenting us by keeping us on the edge of expectation day after day. Each of us is competing for such a perfect prize. Besides, we can't go after other women we should marry because of the way she treats us!"
Then Telemachus said,

"Eurymachus, and all you other suitors, I will say no more and beg you no further. The gods and the people of Ithaca now know my story. So, give me a ship and a crew of twenty men to take me wherever I need to go. I will travel to Sparta and Pylos, searching for my father, who has been missing for so long. Perhaps someone there can tell me something, or maybe a message from the heavens will guide me, as people often hear news in such ways. If I hear that he is alive and on his way home, I will endure the waste you suitors cause for another twelve months. If, however, I hear of his death, I will return at once. I will hold his funeral rites with all due ceremony, build a monument to his memory, and then arrange for my mother to remarry."

With these words, he sat down. Then Mentor, a trusted friend of Odysseus who had been left in charge of everything and had full authority over the servants, rose to speak. He addressed them plainly and honestly.

"People of Ithaca, listen to me! I hope you never again have a kind and good ruler, or one who governs fairly! I hope all your future leaders are cruel and unjust! Why? Because not one of you has remembered Odysseus, who ruled you as if he were your own father! I'm not even half as angry with the suitors. They act with wickedness in their hearts, betting that Odysseus won't return, so they feel free to take over and devour his estate. But as for the rest of you, I am shocked! You all sit still, not even trying to stop these scandalous things from happening! You could stop them if you wanted to, because you are many, and they are few!"
Leiocritus, son of Evenor, answered him.

"Mentor, what is all this foolishness? Are you trying to stir up the people to stop us? It's hard for one man to fight many over their food! Even if Odysseus himself were to attack us while we're feasting in his house, and try his best to drive us out, his wife, who wants him back so badly, would have little to rejoice about. If he fought against such overwhelming odds, the blame would be entirely on him! There's no sense in anything you've said. So now, all of you, go about your business! Let his father's old friends, Mentor and Halitherses, hurry this boy on his journey, if he even goes at all! I don't think he will go. He's more likely to stay right where he is until someone comes and tells him something."

With that, he broke up the assembly, and everyone went back to their own homes. The suitors returned to Odysseus's house.

Meanwhile, Telemachus went alone to the seashore. He washed his hands in the gray waves and prayed to Athena.

"Hear me!" he cried. "You god who visited me yesterday and commanded me to sail the seas in search of my long-missing father! I want to obey your command, but the Achaeans, especially the wicked suitors, are stopping me from doing so!"

As Telemachus prayed, Athena approached him, disguised as Mentor, speaking with his voice.

Athena said,

"If you have your father's spirit, Telemachus, you won't be foolish or cowardly from now on. Odysseus never broke a promise or left a task unfinished. So, if you're truly like him, your journey won't be in vain. But if the blood of Odysseus and Penelope doesn't run in your veins, I don't see how you can succeed. Sons rarely turn out better than their fathers. Most are worse, and few ever improve. Still, since you won't be foolish or cowardly from now on, and you've inherited at least some of your father's wise judgment, I have hope for your mission. But remember this: never associate with those foolish suitors. They have no sense or virtue, and they don't think about the death and destruction that will soon fall upon every single one of them. They will all die on the same day. Your voyage won't be delayed for long. Your father was an old friend of mine, so I will find you a ship and go with you myself. Now, go home and mingle with the suitors. Start preparing provisions for your journey. Make sure everything is well-packed: wine in jars, and barley meal, which sustains life, in leather bags. Meanwhile, I'll go around town and gather volunteers right away. Ithaca has many ships, both old and new. I'll inspect them for you and pick the best one. We'll get it ready and set sail without delay."

When Athena, daughter of Zeus, finished speaking, Telemachus wasted no time following the goddess's instructions. He returned home, feeling gloomy. In the outer courtyard, the suitors were skinning goats and singeing pigs. Antinous immediately approached him, laughing as he took Telemachus's hand.
"Telemachus, my fiery friend,"
Antinous said,

"don't show your anger in words or deeds anymore. Come, eat and drink with us as you used to. The Achaeans will provide everything you need: a ship, and even a hand-picked crew. Then you can sail to Pylos right away and find out news of your noble father."
Telemachus replied,

"Antinous, I can't eat in peace or find any joy with men like you. Wasn't it enough that you wasted so much of my valuable property when I was just a boy? Now I'm older and wiser, and I've grown stronger. Whether I stay here among my people or go to Pylos, I will do you all the harm I can. I will go, and my journey will not be in vain, even though, thanks to you suitors, I have no ship or crew of my own and must travel as a passenger, not a captain."

As he spoke, he pulled his hand away from Antinous. Meanwhile, the other suitors continued preparing dinner around the buildings, mocking and laughing at Telemachus.

One young man said,

"Telemachus means to be the death of us! I suppose he thinks he can bring friends from Pylos or Sparta to help him. He seems set on going to Sparta. Or maybe he'll even go to Ephyra for poison to put in our wine and kill us?"
Another suitor said,

"Perhaps if Telemachus goes on board ship, he'll end up like his father, dying far from his friends. In that case, we'd have plenty to do. We could divide his property among ourselves. As for the house, we can let his mother and the man who marries her have it."

This was how they talked. But Telemachus went down into the high, spacious storeroom. His father's treasures of gold and bronze were piled on the floor there, and linen and spare clothes were kept in open chests. There was also a supply of fragrant olive oil, and casks of old, well-aged wine, pure and fit for a god to drink, were lined up against the wall, just in case Odysseus ever returned home. The storeroom was secured by sturdy doors that opened in the middle. And the faithful old housekeeper, Eurycleia, managed everything day and night. She was the daughter of Ops, son of Pisenor. Telemachus called her to the storeroom and said,

"Nurse, pour me some of the best wine you have, after what you're saving for my father's own drinking. This is in case, poor man, he escapes death and finally makes his way home. Give me twelve jars, and make sure they all have lids. Also, fill some well-stitched leather bags with barley meal, about twenty measures in total. Get all these things ready at once, and don't tell anyone. I'll take everything this evening, as soon as my mother has gone upstairs for the night. I plan to go to Sparta and Pylos to see if I can hear any news about my dear father's return."
When Eurycleia heard this, she began to cry and spoke to him with a loving voice.

"My dear child, what on earth has put such an idea into your head? Where in the world do you intend to go? You are the only hope of this house! Your poor father is dead and gone in some distant, unknown land. The moment your back is turned, these wicked men here will plot to get rid of you and divide all your possessions among themselves. Stay here among your own people. Don't risk your life wandering across the barren ocean."
Telemachus answered,

"Don't worry, Nurse. My plan has the gods' approval. But swear to me that you won't tell my mother about any of this until I've been gone for about ten or twelve days, unless, of course, she hears I'm gone and asks you herself. I don't want her to ruin her beauty by crying."

The old woman solemnly swore she wouldn't. Once her oath was complete, she began pouring wine into jars and putting barley meal into the bags. Meanwhile, Telemachus returned to the suitors.

Then Athena turned her thoughts to another matter. She disguised herself as Mentor and went around town, telling each crew member to meet at the ship by sundown. She also went to Noemon, son of Phronius, and asked him to lend her a ship. Noemon was happy to agree. When the sun set and darkness covered the land, Athena launched the ship and loaded all the necessary equipment onto it. She then anchored it at the end of the harbor. Soon, the crew arrived, and the goddess offered words of encouragement to each of them.

Next, Athena went to Odysseus's house and cast a deep slumber over the suitors. She made their drinks muddle their minds and caused them to drop their cups. So instead of lingering over their wine, they returned to town, their eyes heavy and full of drowsiness, and fell asleep. Then Athena, in the form and voice of Mentor, called Telemachus to come outside.

Athena said,
"Telemachus, the men are on board, oars in hand, waiting for your orders. Hurry, let's go!"
Athena led the way, and Telemachus followed close behind her. When they reached the ship, the crew was waiting by the water's edge. Telemachus said,
"Alright, my men, help me get the supplies on board. They're all gathered in the cloister. My mother knows nothing about this, and neither do any of the maidservants, except for one."

After saying this, Telemachus led the way, and the others followed. Once they had brought the supplies as he instructed, Telemachus boarded the ship. Athena went first, taking her seat in the stern, and Telemachus sat beside her. Then the crew untied the ropes and took their places on the benches. Athena sent them a fair wind from the west. The wind whistled over the deep blue waves. Telemachus told the crew to grab the ropes and hoist the sail, and they did as he commanded. They set the mast into its socket in the cross plank, raised it, and secured it tightly with the forestays. Then, with ropes made of twisted ox hide, they hoisted the white sails high. As the sails swelled with the wind, the ship flew across the deep blue water, and foam hissed against her bow with every surge forward. They secured everything on board, filled the mixing bowls to the brim, and poured out drink offerings to the immortal gods. They offered special thanks to Athena, the grey-eyed daughter of Zeus.

And so, the ship sailed on through the dark hours of the night, until dawn broke.
